Photograph: Dean Sewell/AAP New South Wales NSW should compensate elderly woman whose public housing was inundated with sewage, ombudsman finds Ombudsman finds Homes NSW acted unreasonably and recommended additional payment for distress and suffering Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Achol Arok Fri 31 Jul 2026 11.00 EDT Last modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 22.40 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google An elderly public housing tenant whose home was damaged by sewage overflows will be fully compensated by the New South Wales government after it disposed of her personal belongings without her consent and failed to properly support her insurance claim. The NSW Ombudsman on Friday published its report after an investigation in which it found Homes NSW acted unreasonably in how it handled the tenant’s contaminated belongings and “failed to provide full and accurate information to the insurer”. The woman, whose name and suburb were not made public, had lived in the unit for more than 15 years. She reported three successive sewage overflows within three months, which saw raw sewage enter the property. After the third incident she was relocated, but her belongings remained in the contaminated unit for two months before being boxed up and moved to a vacant property. ‘I would just like to see more people housed’: inside NSW’s social housing changes Read more The furniture, household items, and family heirlooms were not cleaned nor returned to her, despite Homes NSW telling her “she would be actively involved in the decision to keep or dispose of any items”. She was later told “she would be adequately compensated” through an insurance claim, according to the report. When the claim was lodged, the insurer denied liability and offered a small “goodwill” payment. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email The report found Homes NSW’s failure to provide the insurer with “full and accurate information” which contributed to the rejection of the claim. The ombudsman’s recommendations included an apology and full compensation “in accordance with her itemised compensation claim”. It also recommended an additional payment for “the distress and suffering she experienced while trying to resolve her claim over more than five years”. Homes NSW has accepted all of the recommendations and will implement them by next month, according to the report. The senior deputy ombudsman for complaints and investigations, Kate Anderson, said the findings and recommendations come after identifying “inadequate policies and procedures in place”. “There were several points where there was inadequate communication to her about … what next steps were going to follow and then those steps were ultimately not followed,” she said. Anderson said the case demonstrated the importance of ensuring agencies were able to “listen to their complainants”, particularly when they should “have engaged with this particular individual to reach a conclusion on this complaint far earlier”. “This individual actually had very good record of the possessions that she had and the respective value of them, which ultimately was not taken into consideration,” she said. “At all points, people should be treated with courtesy and respect and the situation that materialised here really demonstrated that ultimately by the time it had come to us, the tenant had been trying to resolve it herself with Home NSW for a number of years and hadn’t been able to get an effective resolution.” A spokesperson for Homes NSW said it “sincerely apologises to the tenant affected” and acknowledged “the distress, inconvenience and impact the situation has had on them”. Homes NSW has since introduced “a number of changes to how we deliver maintenance and repairs with the aim of improved tenant satisfaction, including establishing an in-house call centre to manage repair requests”, the spokesperson said. https://www.baltictimes.com/study__diffe.text: Estonia Latvia Lithuania Business Analysis Opinions Culture EU Affairs Search Archive Study: Difference between cheapest and most expensive shopping basket in Estonia was over 12 euros 2026-07-23 BNS/TBT Staff TALLINN - In a July price comparison conducted by market research firm SeeNext, the cheapest shopping basket was found at Lidl, with the price difference to the most expensive basket being a significant 43 percent, or over 12 euros. According to the price comparison conducted by SeeNext at the beginning of July, Lidl was the most affordable among the retail chains surveyed. The average shopping basket at Lidl cost 28.02 euros, while at Coop, which proved to be the most expensive, the same basket cost 40.06 euros. This marks a price difference of 12.04 euros between the cheapest and most expensive baskets. The shopping basket used in the study consisted of 28 of the most commonly consumed products, with the cheapest available option for each item being selected at every store. The selection included various fruits like bananas and apples, vegetables such as potatoes and carrots, as well as dairy, meat, and grain products, and non-alcoholic beverages. "Lidl's goal is to offer products at a good price without compromising on quality. We focus on what people need every day and ensure that the daily shopping basket is as affordable as possible for our customers. A wide selection of private-label products, efficient work processes, a well-thought-out store concept, and close cooperation with producers help us keep costs under control and consistently offer customers a great price-to-quality ratio," said Liisa-Indra Pajuste, Head of Communications at Lidl Estonia. According to the study, Lidl offered the most affordable prices in nearly all categories compared: dairy, meat, grain, and beverage products. Notably, the price difference between the cheapest and most expensive retailer varied by category, ranging from 1.50 euros for beverages to 4.74 euros for dairy products. STUDY METHODOLOGY: During the study, SeeNext mystery shoppers visited stores of the six largest retail chains in Tallinn, Tartu, and Narva: Maxima, Rimi, Lidl, Selver, Grossi, and Coop. A shopping basket was compiled for the study, consisting of 28 of the most commonly used and cheapest everyday food items, including dairy products, meat, grain products, dry goods, fruits and vegetables, and beverages. https://www.delfi.lt/en/business/constru.text: Delfi EN Delfi Business 2026.09.07 15:51 Construction of green hydrogen plant completed in Vilnius Translated by Karolis Broga Source: Elta EN Construction of green hydrogen plant completed in Vilnius PHOTO: Company photo Follow Delfi on Google Construction of a EUR 10 million green hydrogen plant has been completed on the grounds of Vilnius Second Combined Heat and Power Plant. Its equipment and systems are currently undergoing testing, announced district heat supplier Miesto gijos. Meanwhile, a publicly accessible hydrogen refuelling station, the first of its kind in Vilnius, is being installed at the Viršuliškės Public Transport Park. Once the remaining equipment is tested and the refuelling point completed, the production of green hydrogen is expected to begin before the end of 2026. The European Union has earmarked EUR 5.64 million funding for the project, while the remaining amount was allocated by Vilnius City Municipality. Over its five‑year operational period, the plant will be required at least once to produce 1.42 million cubic metres (128,000 kg) of green hydrogen per year. Operating at maximum capacity, its annual production volume should reach 285,000 kg of green hydrogen. In the first stage, 16 public transport buses will be supplied with green hydrogen, which will replace diesel buses. This will allow cutting around 1,400 tonnes of carbon dioxide emissions annually. The plant capacity of 3 megawatts (MW) will be enough for 40 hydrogen-powered buses. Therefore, Vilnius city will be able to expand its ecological public transport fleet. The hydrogen refuelling station will be open to public and may be used not only by city buses but also by commercial transport and individual drivers.
